overview: Solomon Islands includes communities with distinct languages, artistic practices and island histories. Canoe ornaments, feather currency, shellwork and recordings reveal how people made useful objects, exchanged goods and performed together. Independence in 1978 began a new political chapter within much older and continuing cultural histories.

periods.title: Protectorate rule and the path to independence
periods.summary: Britain declared a protectorate in 1893. Debate about independence grew through the 1960s and 1970s, including disagreement over regional interests. Internal self-government in 1976 preceded independence in 1978.

periods.title: An independent Solomon Islands
periods.summary: Solomon Islands became independent on 7 July 1978. National institutions brought diverse island communities into a shared state, while regional identities and creative practices continued.

items.text: A late nineteenth- or early twentieth-century nguzunguzu at the Metropolitan Museum combines blackened wood with nautilus-shell inlay. The collection tentatively attributes it to New Georgia. Its carved face and hands show the close relationship between boat decoration, bodily ornament and spiritual protection.

Such figures were lashed near the base of a canoe's prow rather than carved as a permanent part of the hull. They could be removed, exchanged or transferred between boats. Canoes supported fishing and transport as well as warfare, so their making joined practical skill with ceremonial importance.

The names and interpretations of canoe figures vary between western island communities. Modern artists continue to use their forms as cultural and national symbols. A museum example can illuminate one tradition without representing every community in the country.

Te Papa holds a twentieth-century tevau collected on Peleni in the Santa Cruz Islands in 1969. Specialists attached small red feathers to overlapping platelets and decorated the coil with shell and fiber. Leaves and oilcloth protected this particular example during storage and travel.

Tevau could be exchanged for goods and services, including canoes, crops and pigs, and given in marriage ceremonies. Their value reflected color, condition and skilled labor; fading feathers could reduce it. This was a regional system of valuables, not a single currency used uniformly across all the islands.

In her fieldwork account of Baegu communities on Malaita, Kay Ross described ornaments made from small red, white and black shell discs. Plant fiber joined discs into planned geometric arrangements for belts and armbands. Fine finishing could make both sides presentable.

Ross also described coastal and inland communities exchanging fish and taro. Shell valuables circulated at weddings and feasts, where relatives helped assemble gifts. Her account records particular communities and a particular period, rather than a timeless rule for all Solomon Islanders.

Hugo Zemp's recordings of Fataleka and Baegu music, released in 1973, document bamboo panpipes, clapping sticks, singing and dance. Performances place instruments within funeral and other ceremonial settings, allowing listeners to hear coordination between people as well as individual sounds.

The album identifies Afunakwa as the singer of the lullaby Rorogwela. Other tracks feature women and girls singing or performers playing bamboo instruments. Named performers and recorded contexts help keep an account of music connected to people rather than an anonymous national style.

Internal self-government began on 2 January 1976, followed by constitutional negotiations in London in 1977. Debate included regional finances and the place of the Western Solomons in the new country. Independence emerged through negotiation and disagreement, not a universally shared timetable.

The Independence Order names 7 July 1978 as the appointed day. That document provides a precise date for the political transition, while art objects and recordings document cultural work that both preceded independence and continued afterward.

ending.text: British protectorate rule ended with independence on 7 July 1978. Solomon Islands continues as a country whose communities have varied histories, languages and traditions. The political transition did not end regional identities, exchange relationships or creative practice.
